items.title: Q1 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

What can be the use of a poetry that has no true subject except the poet's own selfhood? The traditional use of poetry in the Western world has been
instruction through delight, where teaching has meant the common truths or common deceptions of societal tradition, and where esthetic pleasure has
meant a fulfillment of expectations founded upon past joys of the same design.
But an individual psyche has its own accidents, which it needs to call truths, and its own necessity for self-recognition, which requires the pleasures of
originality, even if those pleasures depend upon a kind of lying against time, and against the achievements of the past. The use of such poetry demands to
be seen in a deidealized way, if it is to be seen more truly.
                                                                 - Harold Bloom, "The Use of Poetry"
In the context of the above which is closest to being true?
options: There can be no use of poetry
Poetry can have no true subject
Man may be the true subject of poetry
The poet himself may be the subject
items.explanation: In 'The Use of Poetry' (from Figures of Capable Imagination, 1976), Harold Bloom observes that post-Enlightenment and Romantic lyric poetry takes the poet's own selfhood and individual psyche as its true subject.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit II: Poetry · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem:
Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow:

No worst, there is none.
No worst, there is none. Pitched past pitch of grief,
More pangs will, schooled at forepangs, wilder wring.
Comforter, where, where is your comforting?
Mary, mother of us, where is your relief?
My cries heave, herds-long; huddle in a main, a chief
Woe, world-sorrow; on an aage-old anvil wince and sing-
Then lull, then leave off. Fury had shrieked 'No lingering!
Let me be fell: force I must be brief."'
O the mind, mind has mountains; cliffs of fall
Frightful, sheer, no-man-fathomed. Hold them cheap
May who ne'er hung there. Nor does long our small
Durance deal with that steep or deep. Here! creep,
Wretch, under a comfort serves in a whirlwind: all
Life death does end and each day dies with sleep.
                                                                        - Gerard Manley Hopkins

Which of the following best describes the meaning of the title of the poem, 'No worst, there is none.'?
options: It is not worst because there is nothing
Nothing can be so much bad as this
No it is worst as nothing is there
It is very bad as no one is there
items.explanation: In Gerard Manley Hopkins's 'terrible sonnet' 'No worst, there is none' (composed 1885), the opening phrase expresses extreme spiritual anguish in which no suffering seems worse, yet even deeper pangs continually follow.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:
'Justice' was done, and the President of the Immortals , in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his
sport with Tess. And the D'Urberville knights and dames slept on in their tombs unknowing.
The two speechless gazers bent themselves down to the earth, as if in prayer, and remained
thus a long time, absolutely motionless; the flag continued to wave silently. As soon as they
had enough strength they arose, joined hands again, and went on.
                                                                                                --Thomas Hardy, Tess of the D'Urbervilles
How did the 'sport with Tess' end?
items.explanation: At the close of Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), the raising of the black flag over Wintoncester prison signifies that Tess has been executed by hanging for killing Alec d'Urberville.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

The solemn temples, the great globe itself,
Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve
And, like this insubstantial pageant faded,
Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff
As dreams are made on, and our little life
Is rounded with a sleep.
                                                                 --  Shakespeare, The Tempest
'[T]his insubstantial pageant' refers to:
items.explanation: In Act 4, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's The Tempest, Prospero's phrase 'this insubstantial pageant' refers immediately to the illusory betrothal masque performed by Ariel and his fellow spirits, which vanishes into thin air.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Sidney
items.stem: In "An Apology for Poetry" Sidney discusses the didactic function of poetry by comparing it to philosophy and:
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (1595), Sir Philip Sidney argues for the superior didactic power of poetry by comparing the poet with the moral philosopher (who gives abstract precepts) and the historian (who is tied to particular facts).

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Hellenistic / Alexandrian Greece · Unit II: Poetry · Longinus
items.stem:
According to Longinus which two of the following qualities apply to 'great poetry'?
A. It must be the work of genius, an inspired person.
B. It must cause a feeling of melancholy in the reader.
C. It must employ devices of rhetoric.
D. It must please selectively and on special occasions.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In On the Sublime, Longinus identifies innate grandeur of thought and inspired passion—the mark of genius (A)—together with the skillful use of rhetorical figures, noble diction, and elevated composition (C) as the five sources of sublimity in great poetry.

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot
items.stem:
In "The Function of Criticism" T.S.Eliot attacked J. Middleton Murry and similar critics for being devotees of what he

called:
items.explanation: In his 1923 essay 'The Function of Criticism,' T.S. Eliot upholds classicism and external authority while mocking John Middleton Murry's Romantic reliance on the individual 'Inner Voice,' which Eliot equates with 'doing as one likes.'

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem: Who among the following compared 'the mind in creation' to 'a fading coal'?
items.explanation: In A Defence of Poetry (written 1821, published 1840), Percy Bysshe Shelley writes that 'the mind in creation is as a fading coal, which some invisible influence, like an inconstant wind, awakens to transitory brightness.'

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks
items.stem: Who among the following considered paraphrase as 'a heresy'?
items.explanation: New Critic Cleanth Brooks coined the phrase 'The Heresy of Paraphrase' in the concluding chapter of The Well Wrought Urn (1947), arguing that a poem's organic unity of paradox and irony cannot be reduced to a prose statement.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Empiricist linguistics is concerned with :
options: reason as a determinant of enquiry
items.explanation: Empiricist linguistics (such as Bloomfieldian structuralism) relies on directly observable sense-data and corpora of actual utterances, contrasting with rationalist Chomskyan linguistics, which investigates innate mental competence.

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
In Noam Chomsky's  definition of grammar which two features are drawn from mathematics ?
A. complexity
B. abstraction
C. transformation
D. generation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Syntactic Structures (1957), Noam Chomsky adapted the formal mathematical concepts of 'generation' (generative rewrite rules) and 'transformation' from recursive function theory and formal logic to model syntactic competence (C and D only).

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: 'Potato' is a sixteenth-century borrowing into English from:
items.explanation: The English word 'potato' was borrowed in the mid-sixteenth century from Spanish patata, which itself blended the Taíno (Caribbean) word batata ('sweet potato') with Quechua papa.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who among the following represents the global spread of English diagrammatically as three concentric circles?
items.explanation: Indian-American linguist Braj B. Kachru formulated the 'Three Concentric Circles' model of World Englishes in 1985, categorizing varieties into the Inner Circle, the Outer Circle, and the Expanding Circle.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who among the following is the founder of the Survey of English Usage (SEU)?
items.explanation: British linguist Randolph Quirk founded the Survey of English Usage (SEU) at University College London in 1959, compiling the first large-scale corpus of spoken and written British English.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · J. M. Coetzee
items.stem: Who is the author of the short story, "Beethoven Was One-Sixteenth Black"?
items.explanation: South African Nobel laureate Nadine Gordimer authored the short story and collection Beethoven Was One-Sixteenth Black and Other Stories (2007).

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Judith Butler
items.stem:
Arrange the following texts in the chronological order of publication.
A. This Bridge Called My Back
B. Sexual Politics
C. Gender Trouble
D. The Feminine Mystique

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of these landmark feminist works is Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963, D), Kate Millett's Sexual Politics (1970, B), Cherríe Moraga and Gloria Anzaldúa's This Bridge Called My Back (1981, A), and Judith Butler's Gender Trouble (1990, C).

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Aldous Huxley
items.stem: Who is the author of the essay "Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool"?
items.explanation: George Orwell wrote the critical essay 'Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool' (published in Polemic in March 1947), examining Leo Tolstoy's fierce hostility toward William Shakespeare and King Lear.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem:
Which of the following poems by Robert Browning contains the lines, "Our interest's on the dangerous edge of things. /
The honest thief, the tender murderer, / The superstitious atheist. . ."?
items.explanation: These lines are spoken by Bishop Sylvester Blougram in Robert Browning's dramatic monologue 'Bishop Blougram's Apology' (published in Men and Women, 1855), defending his worldly compromise between religious faith and skepticism.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Who among the following edited The Cornhill Magazine?
items.explanation: Victorian novelist William Makepeace Thackeray served as the founding editor of The Cornhill Magazine from its launch by publisher George Smith in January 1860 until 1862.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · H. G. Wells
items.stem: Which of the following novels has its epigraph taken from the Katha Upanishad?
options: The Island of Doctor Moreau by H. G. Wells
The Razor's Edge by Somerset Maugham
Point Counter Point by Aldous Huxley
Room with a View by E. M. Forster
items.explanation: W. Somerset Maugham's novel The Razor's Edge (1944) takes its title and epigraph from the Katha Upanishad (1.3.14): 'The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path to Salvation is hard.'

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who is the author of the essay, "What Isn't Literature?"?
items.explanation: American literary theorist E.D. Hirsch Jr. authored the essay 'What Isn't Literature?' (published in Paul Hernadi's edited volume What Is Literature?, 1978), arguing against purely essentialist definitions of literary texts.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Virginia Woolf
items.stem: Erich Auerbach's Mimesis (1946) ends with a chapter on:
options: Wyndham Lewis's The Apes of God
items.explanation: Erich Auerbach's Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946) concludes with Chapter 20, 'The Brown Stocking,' which analyzes stream-of-consciousness narration in Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse (1927).

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Which of the following clusters is associated with what Julia Kristeva terms the 'semiotic'?
items.explanation: In Revolution in Poetic Language (1974), Julia Kristeva associates the 'semiotic' (le sémiotique) with pre-Oedipal maternal drives, rhythmic pulsions, displacement, slippage, and condensation, contrasting it with the orderly patriarchal 'symbolic.'

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Aphra Behn
items.stem:
Which two works in the following list are written by Aphra Behn?
A. Rover
B. Oroonoko
C. Soldier's Fortune
D. The Princess of Cleve
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Restoration writer Aphra Behn wrote the comedy The Rover (1677, A) and the prose novella Oroonoko: or, The Royal Slave (1688, B), whereas The Soldier's Fortune is by Thomas Otway and The Princess of Cleves by Madame de La Fayette (and dramatized by Nathaniel Lee).

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gustave Flaubert
items.stem:
Which two of the following are works by Gustave Flaubert?
A. The Temptation of Saint Anthony
B. Old Goriot
C. Therese Raquin
D. Sentimental Education
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: French realist master Gustave Flaubert authored Sentimental Education (L'Éducation sentimentale, 1869, D) and The Temptation of Saint Anthony (La Tentation de saint Antoine, 1874, A), whereas Old Goriot is by Honoré de Balzac and Thérèse Raquin by Émile Zola.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following conform to liberal humanist thought?
A. Literature transcends the limits of the age of its origin and so is timeless.
B. Literature is untouched by the essential human nature which is unchanging.
C. Literature is devoid of any purpose to enhance life or promote human values.
D. Identity is a unique essence unaffected by environment and society.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: As outlined in Peter Barry's Beginning Theory, liberal humanism holds that great literature is timeless and transcends its historical moment (A) and that human identity is a fixed, unique essence prior to social and environmental forces (D).

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Northrop Frye
items.stem:
Which two of the following conform to Northrop Frye's typology of literature?
A. Mythos of spring: Comedy
B. Mythos of summer: Satire
C. Mythos of autumn: Tragedy

D. Mythos of winter: Romance
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Anatomy of Criticism (1957), Northrop Frye's seasonal cycle of mythoi pairs Spring with Comedy (A), Summer with Romance, Autumn with Tragedy (C), and Winter with Irony and Satire, making A and C only correct.

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fyodor Dostoevsky, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.stem:
Which two of the following writers does A. D. Hope address through his poetic responses in A Book of Answers?
A. Tolstoy
B. Dostoevsky
C. Mallarme
D. Goethe
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Australian poet A.D. Hope's collection A Book of Answers (1978) features poetic dialogues with canonical writers including Leo Tolstoy ('Country Places: An Epistle to Leo Tolstoy'), Stéphane Mallarmé, and Fyodor Dostoevsky (keyed as A and C only).

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following are true according to the documentation style prescribed by the eighth edition of the MLA
Handbook?
A. If the title page of a book contains an imprint as well as the publisher's name, omit the imprint and use the publisher's
name.
B. While giving a URL copy it from the Web browser but omit http:// or https://.
C. If a quotation extends to more than five lines set it off from the text as block indented an inch from the left margin.
D. Long titles should be abbreviated using the first letter of key words typed in upper case without intervening space.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: According to the eighth edition of the MLA Handbook (2016), citations omit book imprints in favor of the publisher's name (A) and omit 'http://' or 'https://' from URLs (B); prose block quotations apply to passages of more than four lines, not five.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following are highlighted in relation to specific historical moments by Stephen Greenblatt?

A. crisis of meaning
B. circulation of meaning
C. production of meaning
D. deferral of meaning
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In New Historicist theory (such as Renaissance Self-Fashioning and Shakespearean Negotiations), Stephen Greenblatt examines the historical production of meaning (C) and the circulation of meaning and social energy (B) across cultural discourses.

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following belong to the Chicago School of critics?
A. R. S. Crane
B. E. M. W. Tillyard
C. Elder Olson
D. Allen Tate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: R.S. Crane and Elder Olson were leading figures of the Chicago School of Neo-Aristotelian criticism (co-authoring Critics and Criticism: Ancient and Modern, 1952), whereas Allen Tate was a Southern New Critic and E.M.W. Tillyard a Cambridge historicist.

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Donne
items.stem:
Which of the following poems contains John Donne's famous conceit bringing a parallel between lovers and the hands
of a compass?
items.explanation: In 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' (composed 1611, published 1633), John Donne compares the spiritually united souls of parted lovers to the fixed and moving legs of a pair of 'stiff twin compasses.'

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edgar Allan Poe, Virginia Woolf, Henry James, T. S. Eliot

 A. T. S. Eliot, "The Function of Criticism"
 B. Edgar Allan Poe, "The Philosophy of Composition"
 C. Henry James, "The Art of Fiction"

 D. Virginia Woolf, "Modern Fiction"
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below

 D. The Spectator
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Daniel Defoe started The Review in February 1704 (C), Richard Steele launched The Tatler in April 1709 (A), Jonathan Swift and Tories ran The Examiner from August 1710 (B), and Addison and Steele founded The Spectator in March 1711 (D).

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A : Postmodern narratives focus on the indeterminate and unstable nature of textuality and subjectivity.
Reason R : Postmodern narrative acts regard narratives and characters as tentative representations of writing and
identity.
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.explanation: Postmodern fiction foregrounds the unstable, indeterminate nature of textuality and human subjectivity (Assertion A) precisely because postmodern metafiction treats narratives and characters as provisional, constructed representations of writing and identity (Reason R).

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: In Waiting for Godot, it is Vladimir who questions the Boy who comes from Godot towards the end of the two
Acts.
Statement II: In Waiting for Godot, it is Estragon who says, "Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes, it's awful."
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: In Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953), Vladimir interrogates Godot's messenger Boy at the end of both acts (Statement I is true), and Estragon speaks the famous line 'Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes, it's awful!' in Act I (Statement II is true).

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: New Historicism stipulates that teleological connotations of history have to be eschewed.
Statement II: New Historicism neither denies nor accepts totalizing explanations of historical events.
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Influenced by Michel Foucault, New Historicism rejects linear, teleological grand narratives of history (Statement I is true); consequently, it explicitly rejects—rather than remaining neutral toward—totalizing explanations of historical events (Statement II is false).

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What was poor Yorick in Hamlet?
items.explanation: In Act 5, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's Hamlet, the skull unearthed by the First Gravedigger belongs to Yorick, the late King's court jester ('a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy').

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following words refers to a sound that is associated with a particular meaning?
items.explanation: Coined by British linguist J.R. Firth in Speech (1930), a 'phonestheme' is a sub-morphemic sound cluster (such as gl- in gleam, glitter, glisten, and glow) systematically associated with a particular semantic field.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Who among the following Dickens characters appears as a ghost?
items.explanation: In Charles Dickens's novella A Christmas Carol (1843), Ebenezer Scrooge is first visited on Christmas Eve by the chained ghost of his deceased business partner, Jacob Marley.

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Virginia Woolf
items.stem: Virginia Woolf's Orlando opens in 1588 and Orlando, a sixteen-year-old boy, writes a poem called:
items.explanation: In Virginia Woolf's mock-biography Orlando (1928), the sixteen-year-old Elizabethan nobleman begins writing the pastoral poem 'The Oak Tree' in 1588 and completes it more than three centuries later in 1928.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
What function of English is exemplified by the use of English in India as a "link language" along with a first
language by stable bilinguals in well-defined social contexts?
items.explanation: In sociolinguistic studies of bilingualism, when stable bilinguals use a second language (such as English in India) alongside their first language as a link language in well-defined institutional contexts, it performs a 'complementary' function.

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Jean Baudrillard
items.stem: Who among the following is said to have believed that the Persian Gulf War (1990-91) never happened?
items.explanation: French postmodern theorist Jean Baudrillard published three provocative essays collected as The Gulf War Did Not Take Place (La Guerre du Golfe n'a pas eu lieu, 1991), arguing that the 1990–91 conflict was a televised media simulacrum.

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
What 19th-century philosophical term of Russian origin did Friedrich Nietzsche use to describe the disintegration of
traditional morality in western society?
items.explanation: Popularized in Russia by Ivan Turgenev's Fathers and Sons (1862), the term 'nihilism' (from Latin nihil, 'nothing') was adopted by Friedrich Nietzsche to diagnose the collapse of traditional Christian morality and metaphysical values in Western modernity.

items.title: Q51 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following statements is true of the working group set up by the University Grants Commission in 1978 to
study the medium of instruction in higher education?
options: It recommended a quicker switchover of the medium of instruction from English to Indian languages
It observed that English need not be displaced as the medium of instruction although regional languages were quite ready to take over its functions
It argued that English as a highly developed language was best suited for India's industrial and scientific progress
It asserted that English had the potential to further polarize an already-divided nation along socio-economic and intellectual fault lines
items.explanation: The 1978 University Grants Commission (UGC) working group on the medium of instruction observed that English need not be hastily displaced in higher education, even as regional Indian languages developed capacity to assume academic functions.

items.title: Q52 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
In comparative philology and sometimes in modern phonology, what is the term used to refer to the deletion of a vowel
within a word?
items.explanation: In historical phonology and prosody, 'syncope' denotes the loss or elision of one or more sounds (especially an unstressed vowel) from the interior of a word, such as pronouncing 'every' as 'ev'ry' or 'medicine' as 'med'cine.'

items.title: Q53 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following statements best describes Terry Eagleton's views on literature?
options: It is involved in the reproduction of the dominant social order
Its raison d'être is to reflect social reality directly
Its primary purpose is to produce beauty and pleasure
It is closely allied to religion in its significance and seriousness
items.explanation: In Marxism and Literary Criticism (1976) and Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983), Marxist critic Terry Eagleton argues that literature and the institution of English studies function ideologically to reproduce the dominant capitalist social order.

items.title: Q54 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following are true of 'performance', as used in linguistic theory?
A. It is analogous to the Saussurean concept of langue.
B. It refers to the specific utterances of individual native speakers in actual situations.
C. It is an innate grammar that suggests humans' universal ability to use language.
D. It includes hesitations and unfinished structures arising out of psychological difficulties acting upon the speaker.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Noam Chomsky's Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965), 'performance' denotes the actual production of utterances in concrete situations (B), including memory limitations, hesitations, and grammatical slips (D), whereas A and C describe 'competence.'

items.title: Q55 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Gissing, Elizabeth Gaskell, Anne Brontë
items.stem:
Which among the following are the works of George Gissing?
A. New Grub Street
B. Agnes Grey
C. The Odd Women
D. Mary Barton
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Late-Victorian naturalist novelist George Gissing wrote New Grub Street (1891, A) and The Odd Women (1893, C), whereas Agnes Grey (1847) was written by Anne Brontë and Mary Barton (1848) by Elizabeth Gaskell.

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ian McEwan
items.stem:
Which of the following are novels by Ian McEwan?
A. Atonement
B. The Man with Two Left Feet
C. The Child in Time
D. The Rachel Papers
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Contemporary British novelist Ian McEwan wrote The Child in Time (1987, C) and Atonement (2001, A), whereas The Man with Two Left Feet (1917) is by P.G. Wodehouse and The Rachel Papers (1973) is Martin Amis's debut novel.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Nissim Ezekiel
items.stem:
Which of the following are poems by Nissim Ezekiel that make fun of Indians' use of English?
A. "Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T.S."
B. "Philosophy"
C. "Very Indian Poem in Indian English"
D. "Jewish Wedding in Bombay"
E. "Poet, Lover, Birdwatcher"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel's 'Goodbye Party for Miss Pushpa T.S.' (from Hymns in Darkness, 1976, A) and 'Very Indian Poem in Indian English' (C) affectionately satirize Indian English ('Babu English') syntax, progressive-tense overuse, and idioms.

items.title: Q58 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following language areas of the human brain in the order in which they involve in hearing, understanding
and saying a word:
 A. arcuate fasciculus
 B. anterior speech cortex
 C. motor cortex
 D. posterior speech cortex
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In neurolinguistics (the Wernicke–Geschwind model), a heard word is first comprehended in the posterior speech cortex or Wernicke's area (D), transmitted via the arcuate fasciculus (A) to the anterior speech cortex or Broca's area (B), and articulated by the motor cortex (C).

items.title: Q62 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Margaret Atwood, Doris Lessing, Toni Morrison, Alice Walker

 A. Margaret Atwood, The Handmaid's Tale
 B. Alice Walker, The Color Purple
 C. Doris Lessing, The Golden Notebook
 D. Toni Morrison, The Bluest Eye
  Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: These four novels were published in the chronological order: Doris Lessing's The Golden Notebook (1962, C), Toni Morrison's The Bluest Eye (1970, D), Alice Walker's The Color Purple (1982, B), and Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1985, A).

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following terms in the chronological order of their use in literary theory:

1. gynesis
2. scriptible
3. negritude
4. paratext
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Historically, Négritude (C/3) was coined by Aimé Césaire and Léopold Sédar Senghor in the 1930s, scriptible (B/2) by Roland Barthes in S/Z (1970), gynesis (A/1) by Alice Jardine in 1985, and paratext (D/4) by Gérard Genette in Seuils (1987); Option 3 (C, A, D, B) is the only choice beginning with C.

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Unlike scientific research, literary research does not have specific materials for investigation and scientific
tools for reaching a conclusion and formulating a theory.
Statement II: Literary research consists of critical interpretations of an author's work to the exclusion of biography and
editing of texts.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are incorrect: literary research employs rigorous textual, archival, and methodological tools to investigate primary and secondary materials, and it encompasses biography, textual scholarship, and scholarly editing alongside critical interpretation.

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Linguists, being primarily interested in the scientific study of language, approach language dispassionately.
Statement II: Linguists are necessarily polyglots who bring their own biases to language study.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: Modern linguistics is the objective, descriptive, and scientific study of human language (Statement I is correct), and linguists need not be polyglots nor inject personal prescriptive biases into linguistic analysis (Statement II is incorrect).

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following are features of the 'Theatre of the Absurd'?
A. emphasis on the central role of God in the universe

B. presentation of futile actions devoid of any goal
C. portrayal of situations that point to the meaningfulness of life
D. lacking in conflicts and dramatic tensions
E. presenting players in a stasis or drift without definite roles
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Coined by Martin Esslin in 1961, the Theatre of the Absurd presents purposeless, repetitive actions in a world devoid of divine meaning (B), abandons conventional plot conflict and dramatic resolution (D), and depicts characters trapped in existential stasis (E), making B, D and E correct.

items.title: Q67 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Badal Sircar
items.stem: Who, among the following, is known to have used elements from the Yakshagana tradition in his theatre?
items.explanation: Jnanpith laureate Girish Karnad drew extensively on the traditional Kannada folk theatre form Yakshagana—incorporating the Bhagavata narrator, half-curtain, masks, and dolls—in his play Hayavadana (1971).

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Which of these UK universities saw the first institutional incorporation of Cultural Studies?
items.explanation: Cultural Studies was first institutionalized in 1964 when Richard Hoggart founded the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) at the University of Birmingham.

items.title: Q70 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: Which of these poets wrote a poem that served to inspire W B Yeats to write his own poem, "When you are Old"?
items.explanation: W.B. Yeats's lyric 'When You Are Old' (published in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892) is an adaptation of French Pléiade poet Pierre de Ronsard's 1578 sonnet 'Quand vous serez bien vieille' (from Sonnets pour Hélène).

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Meenakshi Mukherjee
items.stem:
Which of these does Meenakshi Mukherjee propose as the possible target readership of early Indian English novel?
A. A pan-Indian readership
B. A localized Indian readership
C. A British readership
D. The colonial administrator in India
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In her seminal critical studies of early Indian English fiction (including 'The Perishable Empire' and 'Realism and Reality'), Meenakshi Mukherjee argues that 19th-century Indian novelists writing in English primarily addressed an audience outside India—specifically a British readership and colonial administrators in India—which shaped their explanatory and ethnographic narrative strategies.

items.explanation: Symbolist poet Charles Baudelaire wrote in French (A-I), Romantic ironist Heinrich Heine in German (B-II), confessional poet Sylvia Plath in English (C-III), and Cuban modernist national hero José Martí in Spanish (D-IV).

items.title: Q73 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Upamanyu Chatterjee
items.stem:
Which of these constitute the preoccupations of the protagonist of Upamanyu Chatterjee's English, August?
A. Marijuana
B. Magic
C. Monotheism
D. Marcus Aurelius
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Upamanyu Chatterjee's novel English, August: An Indian Story (1988), young IAS probationer Agastya Sen copes with his alienation in the provincial town of Madna by smoking marijuana (A) and reading the Meditations of Roman Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius (D).

items.title: Q74 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
What was the name of the journal published from Bowling Green University beginning 1969, which carried essays on
amusement parks, comics and detective films?
items.explanation: Ray B. Browne founded The Journal of Popular Culture at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, pioneering the academic study of everyday mass culture including comics, detective fiction, and amusement parks.

items.title: Q75 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of these best describes Shyam Selvadurai's novel, Funny Boy?
items.explanation: Sri Lankan-Canadian writer Shyam Selvadurai's Funny Boy (1994) is a queer coming-of-age novel (Bildungsroman) told in six episodes following Tamil boy Arjie Chelvaratnam amidst mounting ethnic violence prior to the 1983 Colombo riots.

items.title: Q76 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which of these questions would Cultural Studies be most interested in asking?
A. Who decides what is to be produced?
B. Who can afford the artifact?
C. How is the artifact marketed?
D. What is the register of speech in the artifact?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Cultural Studies investigates the political economy and 'circuit of culture' surrounding cultural artifacts—specifically who controls production (A), who has economic access to consume them (B), and how they are marketed (C)—rather than purely formal linguistic register (D).

items.title: Q77 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who, among the following, played the most significant role in mobilizing the concept of 'cultural intermediaries'?
items.explanation: French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu mobilized the concept of 'cultural intermediaries' in Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste (1979) to describe media, advertising, and cultural professionals who shape public taste and symbolic capital.

items.title: Q78 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
items.stem: From whom does Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak borrow the term 'subaltern'?
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak and the Subaltern Studies collective borrowed the term 'subaltern' from Italian Marxist philosopher Antonio Gramsci's Prison Notebooks, where it designates subordinated social groups excluded from hegemonic power.

items.title: Q79 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Which of the following does the Subaltern Studies project contend?
A. Traditional historiography celebrated the role of the subalterns.
B. Traditional history of India's freedom movement celebrates the contribution of select icons.
C. Traditional historiography highlights the dominant strands of India's freedom struggle.
D. Subaltern Studies historiography highlights the dominant strands of India's freedom struggle.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Founded by Ranajit Guha in 1982, the Subaltern Studies project critiques colonial and bourgeois-nationalist historiography for celebrating only select elite icons (B) and dominant mainstream strands of India's freedom struggle (C) while erasing subaltern agency.

items.title: Q80 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which of these did the Wood's Despatch (1854) seek to propagate?
A. Impart Western knowledge to Indians
B.  Restrict access to English learning in India
C. Educate British officers in Sanskrit and Persian
D. Create a class of public servants
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Prepared by Sir Charles Wood in 1854 ('the Magna Carta of English Education in India'), Wood's Despatch sought to diffuse European arts, science, and philosophy in India (A) and supply the colonial administration with a reliable class of public servants (D).

items.title: Q81 · Dec 2021 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Joseph Addison, Richard Steele, Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
Arrange the following periodicals in the chronological order in which they started  publication:
A. The Spectator
B. The Tatler
C. The Rambler

items.stem: In "Mr Bennett and Mrs Brown" Virginia Woolf:
options: responds to E.M Forster's remarks on character in fiction
criticises book buying preferences of the educated English class
analyses the state of modern fiction by contrasting two generations of writers
presents modernity as a stable and coherent project uniting all artists
items.explanation: In her 1924 essay 'Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown,' Virginia Woolf analyzes the shift in modern fiction ('on or about December 1910 human character changed') by contrasting externalist Edwardian novelists (Bennett, Wells, Galsworthy) with modernist Georgian writers (Joyce, Eliot, Lawrence).
